title: Madeira
description: A volcanic Atlantic island whose wine is heated, oxidised and almost immortal.
L: Madeira is a Portuguese volcanic island in the Atlantic, about 700 km off Morocco. Its mountains rise to over 1,800 m. Vineyards are small, on steep terraces called poios, mostly on the north and south coasts, from sea level to about 800 m. Volcanic basalt soils are fertile and acidic. There are only about 500 hectares of vines.

The climate is subtropical and humid, with mild temperatures all year. The south coast is warmer and drier; the north coast cooler and wetter. Humidity brings disease, so vines are often trained on low pergolas, latadas. Water is channelled from the mountains through levadas, ancient irrigation canals.
Levadas bring water from the mountains to the terraces.

From the 15th century, Madeira was a stop for ships to the Americas and India. Wine loaded as ballast crossed the tropics and came back improved by heat and movement, called vinho da roda, round-trip wine. Spirit was added to protect it. Madeira became the toast of the American colonies; it was used to toast the Declaration of Independence in 1776.
Madeira improved after crossing the tropics by ship.
Yes. Heat and movement transformed it, which producers now recreate.
Madeira is a steep, volcanic Atlantic island
Its humid, subtropical climate needs pergolas and levadas
Ship voyages through the tropics shaped its style

Tinta Negra is a black grape making about 80% of Madeira. It's versatile, used for every sweetness level. Until 2015, it couldn't be named on labels; now it can. Most Madeira labelled by age, like 5 Years Old, is Tinta Negra, unless a noble grape is named.

Four white grapes are called noble, and each traditionally gives a level of sweetness: Sercial, driest; Verdelho, medium dry; Boal, or Bual, medium sweet; Malvasia, or Malmsey, sweetest. A wine named after a noble grape must contain at least 85% of it. Terrantez, rare, is a fifth noble grape, medium dry to medium sweet.
Order the noble grapes from driest to sweetest.
All Madeira keeps striking acidity, even the sweetest Malmsey. That's what makes it so fresh and long-lived.
Tinta Negra makes about 80% of Madeira
Sercial, Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia run from dry to sweet
Named noble grape wines need at least 85% of that grape

Madeira is fortified with grape spirit at 96%, to about 17 to 22% alcohol. For drier styles, like Sercial, spirit is added late, after more fermentation; for sweeter styles, like Malvasia, early. Then the wine is heated, recreating the effect of tropical voyages.

Estufagem heats wine in stainless steel tanks, estufas, to 45 to 50 degrees for at least three months, then rests it. It's faster and cheaper, used for younger wines. Canteiro ages wine in wooden casks in warm lofts, armazéns, for years, sometimes decades, heated only by the sun. Canteiro is slower and gentler, giving finer wines. All top Madeiras are canteiro.
Match each method to its feature.

Madeira's ageing exposes it to heat and oxygen, deliberately. The wine turns amber to brown, with caramel, toffee, nuts, dried fruit, coffee and citrus peel. Because it's already oxidised and heated, it's almost indestructible: once opened, it lasts for months; old bottles from the 18th century can still be sound.
Which method gives Madeira's finest wines?
Estufagem heats tanks for months; canteiro ages casks for years
Heat and oxygen make it almost indestructible

Sercial, grown at higher, cooler sites, gives dry, high-acid wines with citrus and almonds. Verdelho gives medium dry wines, with dried fruit and smoke. Boal gives medium sweet wines, with caramel and raisin. Malvasia, or Malmsey, gives rich, sweet wines, with toffee, coffee and orange peel. All keep high acidity.

Madeira labels show age: 3 years, Finest; 5 years, Reserve; 10 years, Special Reserve; 15 years, Extra Reserve; and 20, 30, 40, 50 years and over. Colheita, or Harvest, comes from a single year, aged at least five years. Frasqueira, or Vintage, comes from a single noble grape and year, aged at least 20 years in cask.
Match each grape to its style.
Each noble grape has its style.

Some of the oldest wines still drinkable come from Madeira: Frasqueiras from the 19th century appear at auction and are often still vibrant. Producers like Blandy's, Barbeito, Henriques & Henriques and D'Oliveiras keep stocks of old wine. Rainwater, a lighter style, was popular in the US.
A Frasqueira Madeira must age at least ____ years in cask.
Twenty years, from a single grape and year.
Sercial, Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia run from dry to rich
Labels show age from 3 years to Frasqueira
Old Madeira can stay vibrant for centuries
Reading Madeira and eating with it

Madeira labels show the style, by sweetness or grape: Dry, Medium Dry, Medium Sweet, Sweet, or Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia; and the age: 5, 10 or 15 Years Old, Colheita or Frasqueira. Canteiro may be noted. Tinta Negra can now be named. The IVBAM, the island's wine institute, certifies each bottle.

Sercial suits consommé, olives, almonds and sushi; Verdelho suits mushroom soups and pâté; Boal suits cheese, nuts and fruit cake; Malvasia suits chocolate, coffee desserts and Christmas pudding. Madeira is also a classic in cooking, like Madeira sauce for beef. Serve at 12 to 16 degrees, drier styles slightly cooler.
Consommé with Sercial; chocolate with Malmsey
Which Madeira suits dark chocolate desserts?
An open bottle of Madeira keeps for months. It's the ideal wine to keep on hand for an occasional glass.
Madeira must be finished within a day of opening.
Not true. It's already oxidised, so it keeps for months.

Why does Madeira last so long once opened?
